interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A refresher lesson in eleven screens on the design current Ib, with Back and Continue between them. Screen 1, Do you still have it?: "A 20 kW three-phase heater on a 400 V supply, power factor 1, efficiency 100%. What is its design current, Ib?" Three choices, in this order: 28.87 A, 50.00 A, 86.96 A. Right gives "Still there.", the working 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 400) = 28.87 A, and a line naming the other two as the usual slips: 50.00 A leaves out √3, and 86.96 A works it at 230 V. Two buttons follow. Refresh the why goes on to screen 2, and Skip to the practice goes straight to screen 7. Wrong names the slip, shows the right working and goes on to screen 2, with no skip offered. For 50.00 A it says the heater was treated as one line at 400 V carrying all of it. Three-phase power is √3 × UL × IL × power factor, so the rule divides by √3 × the line voltage. For 86.96 A it says the heater was treated as a single-phase load on 230 V. Screen 2, What it is for: design current is the current a circuit carries in normal service.[^1] The device and the cable are chosen from it, Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz.[^2] Every check after them starts from that choice. If it is skipped or wrong, every later step starts from the wrong current. Screen 3, The why: the same 20 kW output at 400 V. Two sliders, Efficiency and Power factor, run from 0.70 to 1.00 in steps of 0.01. Both open at 1.00, with "Drag either one, or Replay". The opening text: the cable carries what the load draws from the supply. P in the rule is the load's output, so the rule divides by the efficiency to add the losses back.[^18][^17] Reactance, behind the power factor, adds to the draw too.[^21] Three bars sit on one scale that fits the largest, 40.81 kVA at the lowest settings. Each shows its value: Output, 20.00 kW, fixed; Input = output ÷ efficiency, in kW; Apparent = input ÷ power factor, in kVA. The bars use the kit's area colours, not the teal kept for labels. A large readout shows Ib = apparent × 1000 ÷ (√3 × 400), with its working under it. Each figure is worked from the rounded figure above it, to 2 decimal places. At 1.00 and 1.00: 20.00 kW, 20.00 kVA, 28.87 A. At efficiency 0.87 and power factor 0.80: 22.99 kW, 28.74 kVA, 41.48 A (41.47 A when cut short). At 0.70 and 0.70: 28.57 kW, 40.81 kVA, 58.90 A. The sentence under the bars says what stretched which, and keeps its space as it changes. So does the red note. The red note: if it's skipped, the cable is sized on 28.87 A when the load draws the readout's Ib, and that puts the circuit's operation and safety at risk.[^3] One line says real, apparent and reactive power get their own lesson in AC circuits, lesson 8. Here they only show where the extra current comes from. Screen 4, Check, with new numbers so it cannot be answered from the readout just seen: a 7.5 kW three-phase motor on a 400 V supply, power factor 0.85, efficiency 90%. What is Ib? Choices: 12.03 A (power factor left out), 12.74 A (efficiency left out) and 14.15 A (right: 7 500 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.9 × 0.85)). Each wrong one gets a short hint naming the factor left out. A Why? button gives the rule.[^17] Screen 5, The voltage at the board, and diversity: a sub-board given as 393 V. 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 393) = 29.38 A, against 28.87 A at 400 V.[^4] A given voltage must be used. At a sub-board it is lower than 400 V because of the submain's voltage drop.[^5][^6] The text says once that we assume the load still takes its full power. That is near enough for a motor driving its load, which draws more current at a lower voltage.[^29] A plain heater really draws a little less, so for a heater the figure errs on the safe side.[^28] Diversity in a few short lines: the On-Site Guide's percentages are guidance and need not be applied.[^7] On a domestic lighting circuit its Appendix A allows 66%.[^27] So ten 100 W lamps may be designed at 10 × 100 × 0.66 = 660 W rather than 1000 W.[^8] Lesson 2 does more. Screen 6, Worked example: the same 20 kW load worked three ways, each built a step at a time as the rule builds it, one step shown at each press. 20 kW at 400 V: √3 × 400 = 692.82, then 20 000 ÷ 692.82 = 28.87 A. The same at power factor 0.8 and efficiency 87%: √3 × 400 = 692.82, × 0.87 × 0.8 = 482.20, then 20 000 ÷ 482.20 = 41.48 A. The same at a 393 V sub-board: √3 × 393 = 680.70, then 20 000 ÷ 680.70 = 29.38 A. Then one line: 28.86 A and 41.47 A, where he sees them printed, are cut short rather than rounded, and nothing changes. Screen 7, Section A, question 1 (a): the showroom's scenario panel[^9][^10][^11] and "(a) Determine the design current." A typed answer (part 1a): 11 000 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.86 × 0.8) = 23.08 A. 23.10 A (√3 taken as 1.73) is also accepted. Any accepted answer other than 23.08 A is told it is within rounding, and that part (b) starts from 23.08 A. Each usual slip gets its own hint: 15.88 A (efficiency and power factor left out), 18.46 A (power factor left out), 19.85 A (efficiency left out), 39.97 A (√3 left out), 69.51 A (the single-phase rule at 230 V). After two wrong tries, the working is shown. Screen 8, Section A, question 1 (b): (a) carried forward at 23.08 A, and "(b) Determine the current in each winding when the motor runs in delta." A small drawing shows three windings joined in a triangle. The line current, 23.08 A, comes in on L1 at one corner, with L2 and L3 at the other two. One winding is marked "?". A typed answer (part 1b): 23.08 ÷ √3 = 13.33 A. 13.32 A (from the unrounded Ib), 13.34 A and 13.35 A (√3 taken as 1.73) are also accepted. Slips: 39.98 A (multiplied by √3), 7.69 A (divided by 3). The feedback: in a balanced delta, the line current is the winding current × √3.[^12] So each winding carries the line current ÷ √3. The showroom's motor has a star-delta starter.[^30] That runs six wires to the motor, one to each end of each winding.[^31] So in delta each of those cables carries one winding's current. Lesson 3 sizes them, as question 4b asks. An accepted answer other than 13.33 A is told it is within rounding. Screen 9, Section B: "Explain why Ib for a final circuit fed from a sub-board is worked at the voltage at that board, not at 400 V." His written answer is marked against four points (a full answer makes any three), with one more go, then the model answer. Screen 10, Section A, changed numbers: "A three-phase 15 kW oven is fed from a sub-board whose voltage is given as 396 V. Determine the design current." A typed answer: 15 000 ÷ (√3 × 396) = 21.87 A. 21.90 A (√3 taken as 1.73) is also accepted. Slips: 21.65 A (worked at 400 V, not the board's 396 V), 37.88 A (√3 left out). Screen 11, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson. The card holds what it is for, the rule with each formula kept on one line, the voltage to use when none is given, the delta rule, the traps, the showroom's figures so far, and where it lives. A line under the lesson, "Each line is worked from the rounded figure before it.", shows only on the screens with working (3 to 8 and 10).
interactive.ignores: The bars treat the load as balanced across the three lines, as the three-phase rule does. An unbalanced load draws a different current in each line. Efficiency and power factor are fixed numbers here, as a nameplate gives them at full load. A motor running lightly loaded has a lower power factor and efficiency than its nameplate says. Ib is the steady running current. A motor draws much more for a moment as it starts, and lesson 3 allows for that when it chooses the device. The bars show sizes only, not the power triangle. The apparent power is the input divided by the power factor, not the input with something added end to end. At a sub-board, Ib is worked as if the load still takes its full power at the lower voltage. That is near enough true of a motor driving the same load. A plain heater really draws a little less there, so the figure errs on the safe side.

explain.text:
The design current, Ib, is the current a circuit carries in normal service.[^16] The cable carries what the load draws from the supply, not what it gives out. So work Ib from what the load takes in. The rule is Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × efficiency × power factor).[^17] P is the load's output in watts, the figure on its nameplate.[^18] UL is the line voltage, 400 V on a standard three-phase supply.[^14]

Start with the efficiency. [[Efficiency]] is the output divided by the input.[^19] Turn that round and the input is the output divided by the efficiency.[^20] At 87%, 20 kW out needs 20 ÷ 0.87 = 22.99 kW in. The difference is lost inside the machine, but it comes down the cable first. Dividing by the efficiency puts those losses back in.

Then the [[power factor]]. A motor needs more current than its output suggests, because of reactance.[^21] The power factor is the real power in kW divided by the apparent power in kVA that the supply gives.[^22] For an inductive load such as a motor, it is below 1.[^23] So the kVA is bigger than the kW. So the apparent power is the input divided by the power factor: 22.99 ÷ 0.8 = 28.74 kVA.

The line current follows the apparent power. Three-phase real power is √3 × line voltage × line current × power factor.[^24] Turn that round: 28.74 × 1000 ÷ (√3 × 400) = 41.48 A. Do both divisions at once and you have the rule above. Work it from the output alone and you get 28.87 A. A cable sized on 28.87 A for a 41.48 A load puts the circuit's operation and safety at risk.[^3]

Two more things set the number. The first is the voltage at the board. If you are given the voltage at the board, use it.[^5] At a sub-board it is lower than 400 V, because the submain drops some on the way.[^6] We assume the load still takes its full power there. Power is √3 × voltage × current × power factor, so the same power at a lower voltage needs more current. At a 393 V sub-board, 20 kW is 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 393) = 29.38 A.[^4] At 400 V it is 28.87 A. That assumption holds near enough for a motor driving its load. A motor draws more current at a lower voltage.[^29] A plain heater really draws a little less at a lower voltage.[^28] So for a heater, the figure errs on the safe side.

The second is diversity. It is guidance, not a rule. The percentages are in the On-Site Guide, and you need not apply them.[^7] For domestic lighting, Appendix A of the On-Site Guide allows 66%.[^27] So ten 100 W lamps could be designed at 660 W rather than 1000 W. BS 7671 itself has no diversity table. It has the designer assess maximum demand, and it lets diversity be taken into account.[^25]

Now your showroom's motor. Its 11 kW at 400 V is 15.88 A on its output alone. At 86% efficiency and power factor 0.8, it draws 11 000 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.86 × 0.8) = 23.08 A. **Size from what the circuit draws: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × efficiency × power factor).**[^17] **Work it at the voltage at the board.**

analogy.text: Think of ordering cable for a run. The run on the drawing is the output. What you order also has to cover the offcuts and the tails. So the order is the run divided by the share of the drum that ends up in place. Ib works the same way. Divide the output by the share that comes out as useful power, the efficiency. Then divide again by the power factor.
analogy.breaks: Offcuts are gone for good, like the losses inside a motor. The reactive power behind a low power factor is not used up. It surges back and forth between the supply and the motor's magnetic field every cycle. But the current that carries it still flows in the cable and heats it. That is why Ib counts it.

practice.text:
- Find the output P in watts. Take the efficiency and power factor from the nameplate or the maker's data. A load with nothing to allow for, such as a 20 kW heater, is worked with both as 1.[^13]
- Find the voltage at the board that feeds the circuit. That is 400 V three-phase or 230 V single-phase, unless you are given another value. If you are, use it.[^5]
- Apply the rule. Three-phase: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × efficiency × power factor).[^17] Single-phase: the same without the √3, at the single-phase voltage.
- Apply diversity only where it makes sense. Use the On-Site Guide's figures, as guidance.[^7]
- Carry Ib forward. The device's rating In must be no less than Ib.[^26] The cable's capacity Iz comes next: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz.[^2]

**Rule of thumb:** the cable carries the input, not the output. If the efficiency or the power factor is below 1, Ib is bigger than P ÷ (√3 × UL).

**Worked example:** your showroom's 400 V three-phase 11 kW motor, power factor 0.8 lagging, efficiency 86%.[^11] Ib = 11 000 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.86 × 0.8) = 23.08 A. In a balanced delta, the line current is the winding current × √3.[^12] So each winding carries 23.08 ÷ √3 = 13.33 A. Take √3 as 1.73 and Ib comes to 23.10 A.[^15] That is the same answer to within a few hundredths.

**Common mistakes**
- Sizing on the output alone: 28.87 A for a load that draws 41.48 A.
- Using 230 V or 400 V by habit when the board's voltage is given: 20 kW is 29.38 A at 393 V.
- Leaving out √3: 20 000 ÷ 400 = 50.00 A.
- Working a three-phase load at 230 V: 20 000 ÷ 230 = 86.96 A.
- Treating diversity as a rule. It is guidance.

b1.q: Explain why Ib for a final circuit fed from a sub-board is worked at the voltage at that board, not at 400 V.

points.text: The submain drops some voltage, so the sub-board sits below 400 V.
At the same power, a lower voltage means a larger current, since Ib = P ÷ (√3 × U).
The device and the cable are chosen so that Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz. Worked at 400 V, both would be picked on too small a current.
For example, 20 kW is 28.87 A at 400 V but 29.38 A at 393 V.

b1.model: The submain from the main board drops some voltage, so the sub-board sits below 400 V. We assume the load takes the same power there. Since Ib = P ÷ (√3 × U), a lower voltage gives a larger current. For example, 20 kW is 28.87 A at 400 V but 29.38 A at 393 V. The device and the cable are chosen so that Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz. Worked at 400 V, both would be picked on too small a current. A plain heater really draws a little less, so for a heater the figure errs on the safe side.

summary.title: Design current, Ib
summary.for: The current the circuit carries in normal service. You choose the protective device and the cable from it. Every later check starts from there.
summary.rule:
Single-phase: Ib = P ÷ (U × eff × pf)
Three-phase: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × eff × pf)

P is the output in watts.
U is the voltage at the board if you are given one. Otherwise use 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase.
A plain heater is worked with eff and pf both as 1. For a motor, take them from the nameplate or the maker's data.
In delta, each winding carries the line current ÷ √3.

traps.text: Sizing on the output alone: 28.87 A where the load draws 41.48 A.
Using 230 V or 400 V by habit when the board's voltage is given.
Treating diversity as a rule. It is guidance, from the On-Site Guide.

applied.problem: Screens 5 and 10 and Section B say a lower board voltage needs more current, which holds only if the load takes the same power; a resistive heater at a lower voltage draws less current, so the slides' method is safe-side, not exact. Unstated.

Screen 2 says every later check is sized from Ib, but the fault checks (Zs, adiabatic) are worked from the device and the fault current, not from Ib; they follow from the choice Ib sets, not from Ib itself.
Same overclaim on the Keep this card: the fault checks are not sized from Ib; the device and cable are chosen from it and the later checks start from that choice.
